newsitem.title: JAPAN: Details of Japan's new system in Sunday's election.
newsitem.headline: Details of Japan's new system in Sunday's election.

text.p: Japan voted for the first time on Sunday under a complex electoral system combining first-past-the-post contests with proportional representation.
Here is a guide to the new system, the workings of Japan's parliament and a rough schedule of the voting.

Five hundred members of the Lower House will be chosen in the polls, the first since July 1993 and the first electoral test for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. Japan's old electoral system, under which party colleagues battled each other in multi-seat constituencies, was changed because of concern it encouraged lavish campaigning and party in-fighting.

LOWER HOUSE: The Lower House, or the House of Representatives, is the decisive parliamentary chamber, with power over the Upper House in naming the prime minister, ratifying treaties and passing state budget bills. The prime minister must be a member of the Lower House.
Under a revised law, the new Lower House will have 500 members, down from 511 in the outgoing chamber.

Members serve four years but the prime minister can dissolve the house any time. The 252-member Upper House cannot be dissolved, and half of that chamber is elected every three years for fixed six-year terms.

NEW SYSTEM: Under the new electoral system, 300 Lower House members will be elected in single-seat districts and 200 chosen through proportional representation in 11 regional blocs. At polling stations, voters are given two ballots, one for a candidate in the constituency and one for a party in the regional blocs.

SINGLE-SEAT CONSTITUENCIES: There are 300 new single-seat districts that replace the 129 multi-seat constituencies of the old system. The old system had been blamed as a cause of corruption because candidates were required to spend lavishly on campaigns, many against rivals from the same party. The aim of the new system was to lessen the financial burden on candidates and make it more of a contest between parties and their policies, rather than between candidates. But voters will still cast ballots for a candidate.

PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION: Candidates running in any single-seat constituency can also be listed for the proportional representation section of the vote, meaning they might still be made Lower House members even if they fail in a first-past-the-post contest.
Winners in the single-seat constituencies will be automatically deleted from the proportional representation list. Voters will cast ballots for a party.

October 20: Polls opened at 7.00 a.m. (2200 GMT) and close at 6.00 p.m. (0900 GMT). First exit poll released at 6.00 p.m. (0900 GMT), and final results by about 2.00 a.m. Monday October 21 (1700 GMT Sunday).

Depending on the outcome, the winning bloc, either a party or a coalition, would have between one and two weeks to nominate a candidate for prime minister to be chosen at a Special Session of Parliament. The winner forms a cabinet, normally consisting of 20 members.
